ranking.note: Raised to P1: a hang in kernel log callbacks is a reliability failure that already bites binding users, the most consequential concrete defect on this list.
Raised to P1 and moved up: it addresses the identical deadlock as #36768 and the two must be banded and reviewed together as competing approaches.

Raised to P1: the LevelDB exclusive lock blocks the flagship external-reader use case (Electrs/Esplora) for the library, and the paused design question needs a decision; placed behind the deadlock pair because its benefit is less certain.

Moved up: silently continuing on corrupt point reads is a stability/correctness problem surfaced through the kernel's fatal-error notifications, a stronger problem than the interface-polish P2s below it.
Moved down to sit after its prerequisites #29256 and #33847; it cannot be reviewed usefully ahead of them.
Moved down: useful determinism/multi-instance work, but no dependents and less consequence than the error-handling and logging clusters above.
Moved down: build-target separation is core decoupling work but purely internal, with no consumer-visible effect, so it trails the boundary-behaviour P2s.

inconsistencies: #36768 and #34775 fix the same logging-callback deadlock by different means (#36768 is explicitly described as an alternative to #34775). Review #36768 first and treat the pair as one decision; only one should land.

#34775 (restrict to a single process-wide logging connection, level on the handle) points the API in the opposite direction from #33847/#30342 (multiple per-context connections with per-connection levels). That direction must be settled before either side merges, or one will have to be reworked.

Logging chain order matters: #29256 (context arguments for log macros) and #33847 (connections attached to contexts, itself on #34374) both precede #30342. Reviewing #30342 before its bases is wasted effort.

Error-handling-at-the-boundary cluster overlaps substantially: #29700 (return error status instead of AbortNode), #35646 (remove M_ERROR, use util::Expected), #36326 (typed fatal/flush errors replacing bilingual_str). They rewrite the same code paths; a coordinated plan is needed, and #35646 must precede #35570, which depends on it.

#34132 makes additional read paths fatal through the kernel fatal-error notification while #29700/#36326 change how fatal errors are represented and delivered; whichever lands first forces rebasing of the other's notification surface.
#32427 replaces BlockTreeDB entirely, which would obsolete part of #34132's LevelDB read-failure handling for the block tree; note the overlap when scheduling.
#36739 sits on base PR #36738, which is not in this list; its reviewability as a standalone unit depends on that base.
result.notes: The category is dominated by three interdependent clusters (kernel logging, fatal-error propagation at the boundary, and build/ownership decoupling) rather than independent PRs; banding was kept broad so the clusters do not all collapse into one level. P1 is reserved for the concrete library-consumer failures (callback deadlock) and the one PR that unblocks the external-reader use case. Several PRs here (#34132, #35662, #35570, #36318) substantively touch validation as well as the kernel boundary and would likely benefit from being reviewed with validation reviewers present.
